Use the Weave documentation at https://docs.wandb.ai/weave to answer this question:

How do tracing, evaluations, and Signals fit together?
output.answer:
In short: tracing records what your agent or LLM app does. Evaluations score it against curated, repeatable test cases. Signals automatically score real production traffic. Evaluations and Signals both score outputs, but on different inputs: evaluations use fixed test cases, while Signals use live traffic.

**1. Tracing: what happened**
- Weave's tracing is built on Ops, Calls, Traces and Threads [S3]. A **Call** is one logged run of an Op (a tracked function). It records inputs, output, timing, nesting and errors [S11]. A **Trace** is the full tree of Calls that share one execution context [S5].
- Weave describes Calls as providing the data for debugging, analysis and evaluation [S11].
- Agent integrations, such as the OpenAI Agents SDK, Google ADK or Claude Code, record sessions, turns, LLM calls and tool calls, and show them in the **Agents** view. LLM-app integrations record Calls in the **Traces** view instead [S7].

**2. Evaluations: how well it works on known test cases**
- An `Evaluation` object combines a dataset of test examples with one or more scoring functions. You run it against a model or function, and each `.evaluate()` call is one evaluation run [S2].
- Use evaluations to measure performance on repeatable test cases, compare changes over time and catch regressions (drops in quality after a change) [S2].

**3. Signals: how it behaves in production**
- In the Agents view, the **Signals** tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. Signals score agent turns (one user–agent exchange) and surface quality and safety issues in production [S1, S4].
- To open it, select your project, choose **Agents** in the sidebar, then choose **Signals** [S6].
- A **rating** is a score from 0.0 to 1.0, and **tags** are labels such as "user-frustration". Both are assigned to matching spans [S4]. Weave notes that Calls are similar to OpenTelemetry spans [S11].
- Turns are scored by an LLM judge, or by a remote scorer, which is an HTTP endpoint you host [S1].
- The older Monitors pages describe an earlier version of this production scoring. For new work, Weave points you to Signals in the Agents view [S8, S10].

**How they fit together:** tracing provides the recorded data. Evaluations measure changes against curated examples. Signals score live agent behavior and point you to the traces that need attention [S1, S2, S11]. The older Monitors docs also describe using signal scores and failure analyses to find weaknesses and guide model improvements [S8].

# Evaluations overview

> Evaluation-driven LLM application development to systematically improve applications

*Evaluation-driven LLM application development* helps you systematically improve LLM applications by measuring their behavior using consistent, curated examples.

This guide shows you how to set up and run evaluations in Weave so you can measure your LLM application's performance against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and identify regressions. It's intended for developers building LLM applications who want to move beyond ad hoc testing into a structured, measurable workflow.

**Python**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or list of dictionaries for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).
* Optional configuration like [input preprocessing](#format-dataset-rows-before-evaluating).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against a [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) object or any custom function containing LLM application logic. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

**TypeScript**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or array of objects for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against any function wrapped with `weave.op`. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The TypeScript SDK uses function-based models and scorers. Class-based `Model` and `Scorer` types are not yet available in TypeScript.

To get started with evaluations, complete the following steps:

1. [Create an `Evaluation` object](#create-an-evaluation-object)
2. [Define a dataset of examples](#define-a-dataset-of-test-examples)
3. [Define scoring functions](#define-scoring-functions)
4. [Define a model or function to evaluate](#define-a-model-or-function-to-evaluate)
5. [Run the evaluation](#run-the-evaluation)

After completing these steps, you'll have a reusable evaluation configuration and an evaluation run whose results you can inspect in the Weights & Biases UI. For a complete evaluation code sample, see the [full evaluation code example](#full-evaluation-code-example). You can also learn more about [advanced evaluation features](#advanced-evaluation-usage) like [Saved views](#saved-views) and [Imperative evaluations](#imperative-evaluations-evaluationlogger).

# Integrations overview

> Trace agents and LLM applications with Weave's integrations for agent SDKs, harnesses, LLM providers, and orchestration frameworks.

Weave provides two ways to integrate with your AI stack:

* **Trace agents**: for multi-turn agentic applications built with agent SDKs (such as the OpenAI Agents SDK or Google ADK) or run inside agent harnesses (such as Claude Code, Codex, or Pi.dev). These integrations capture sessions, turns, LLM calls, and tool calls, and render them in the Weave **Agents** view.
* **Trace LLM applications**: for code that calls LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, and others) or uses orchestration frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, DSPy, and others). These integrations capture individual LLM calls and pipeline steps as Weave **Calls** in the **Traces** view.

If you're not sure which path to take, start with [Trace your agents](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/trace-agents.md) for new multi-turn agent work, or [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) for existing LLM-call workflows.

# Monitor using built-in signals

> Weights & Biases provides built-in scoring solutions for agents in production

> [!NOTE]
>
> This page covers a previous approach to monitoring production traffic. For new implementations, use **Signals** under Weave for Agents. See [View agent signals](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-signals.md).

Standard system metrics like latency, token count, and cost don't fully capture agent behavior. Inspecting individual traces provides deep insight but doesn't scale to the millions of traces generated in a live environment.

Signals provide a high-level monitoring solution to this problem by offering automated, behavioral scoring for agents in production:

* Automated scoring: Every incoming production trace is automatically processed and scored on common quality issues and errors.
* Infrastructure: Processing is powered by CoreWeave compute and CoreWeave GPUs for scalability across millions of traces.

By using signals within production, you can:

* Gain behavioral insight. Move beyond system metrics to understand if your agent is hallucinating, failing to follow conversation patterns, or losing grounding in its evidence.
* Accelerate the research loop. Use the scores and failure analyses generated by signals to identify weaknesses, which you can use to research model improvement, data annotation, or reinforcement learning.

## Signals and custom monitors

Use [signals](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/monitors.md), preset automated scorers for production traces, to get started with production monitoring quickly, then add custom monitors for evaluation criteria specific to your application.

| | Signals | Custom monitors |
| - | - | - |
| **Configuration** | One-click enable, no prompt writing | Full control over scoring prompt, model, and parameters |
| **Scope** | Preset quality and error classifiers | Any evaluation criteria you define |
| **Trace selection** | Automatic (successful root traces for quality, failed traces for errors) | Configurable operations, filters, and sampling rate |
| **Model** | Serverless Inference (preset) | Any commercial or Serverless Inference model |
| **Use case** | Quick production monitoring with proven classifiers | Custom evaluation criteria specific to your application |

# Set up custom monitors

> Passively score production traffic to surface trends and issues

> [!NOTE]
>
> Custom monitors are the previous approach to monitoring production traffic. For new implementations, use **Signals** under Weave for Agents. See [View agent signals](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-signals.md).

This page shows you how to set up custom monitors in Weave so you can passively score production traffic and surface trends and issues in your LLM applications. Use this guide when you want to define your own evaluation criteria, beyond Weave's preset signals, for production traces.

Monitors use LLM judges to passively score production traffic to surface trends and issues in your LLM applications. For example, you can monitor your application's responses for correctness or helpfulness, or you can monitor user input to identify trends in what users ask your agents about. Monitors automatically store all scoring results in Weave's database, so you can analyze historical trends and patterns.

You can monitor text, images, and audio in your application's input and output.

Monitors require no code changes to your application. Set them up using the Weights & Biases UI.

If you need to actively intervene in your application's behavior based on scores, use [guardrails](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/guardrails.md) instead.

To score calls with an HTTP endpoint that you host instead of an LLM judge, see [Score Calls with remote scorers](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/remote-scorers.md).

sources.heading: Calls
sources.text:
## Calls

A **Call** is a logged execution of an Op. Every time an Op runs, Weave creates a Call that captures:

* Input arguments
* Output value
* Timing and latency
* Parent-child relationships (for nested calls)
* Any errors that occur

Calls show up as **Traces** in the Weights & Biases UI and provide the data for debugging, analysis, and evaluation. For the full Call object structure and properties, see the [Call schema reference](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/call-schema-reference.md).

Calls are similar to spans in the [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io) data model. A Call can:

* Belong to a Trace, a collection of Calls in the same execution context.
* Have parent and child Calls, forming a tree structure.

# Integrations overview

> Trace agents and LLM applications with Weave's integrations for agent SDKs, harnesses, LLM providers, and orchestration frameworks.

Weave provides two ways to integrate with your AI stack:

* **Trace agents**: for multi-turn agentic applications built with agent SDKs (such as the OpenAI Agents SDK or Google ADK) or run inside agent harnesses (such as Claude Code, Codex, or Pi.dev). These integrations capture sessions, turns, LLM calls, and tool calls, and render them in the Weave **Agents** view.
* **Trace LLM applications**: for code that calls LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, and others) or uses orchestration frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, DSPy, and others). These integrations capture individual LLM calls and pipeline steps as Weave **Calls** in the **Traces** view.

If you're not sure which path to take, start with [Trace your agents](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/trace-agents.md) for new multi-turn agent work, or [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) for existing LLM-call workflows.

# Monitor using built-in signals

> Weights & Biases provides built-in scoring solutions for agents in production

> [!NOTE]
>
> This page covers a previous approach to monitoring production traffic. For new implementations, use **Signals** under Weave for Agents. See [View agent signals](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-signals.md).

Standard system metrics like latency, token count, and cost don't fully capture agent behavior. Inspecting individual traces provides deep insight but doesn't scale to the millions of traces generated in a live environment.

Signals provide a high-level monitoring solution to this problem by offering automated, behavioral scoring for agents in production:

* Automated scoring: Every incoming production trace is automatically processed and scored on common quality issues and errors.
* Infrastructure: Processing is powered by CoreWeave compute and CoreWeave GPUs for scalability across millions of traces.

By using signals within production, you can:

* Gain behavioral insight. Move beyond system metrics to understand if your agent is hallucinating, failing to follow conversation patterns, or losing grounding in its evidence.
* Accelerate the research loop. Use the scores and failure analyses generated by signals to identify weaknesses, which you can use to research model improvement, data annotation, or reinforcement learning.

Monitors use LLM judges to passively score production traffic to surface trends and issues in your LLM applications. For example, you can monitor your application's responses for correctness or helpfulness, or you can monitor user input to identify trends in what users ask your agents about. You can monitor text, images, and audio in your application's input and output.

Monitors require no code changes to your application. Set them up using the Weights & Biases UI.

## Calls

A **Call** is a logged execution of an Op. Every time an Op runs, Weave creates a Call that captures:

* Input arguments
* Output value
* Timing and latency
* Parent-child relationships (for nested calls)
* Any errors that occur

Calls show up as **Traces** in the Weights & Biases UI and provide the data for debugging, analysis, and evaluation. For the full Call object structure and properties, see the [Call schema reference](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/call-schema-reference.md).

Calls are similar to spans in the [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io) data model. A Call can:

* Belong to a Trace, a collection of Calls in the same execution context.
* Have parent and child Calls, forming a tree structure.

# Evaluations overview

> Evaluation-driven LLM application development to systematically improve applications

*Evaluation-driven LLM application development* helps you systematically improve LLM applications by measuring their behavior using consistent, curated examples.

This guide shows you how to set up and run evaluations in Weave so you can measure your LLM application's performance against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and identify regressions. It's intended for developers building LLM applications who want to move beyond ad hoc testing into a structured, measurable workflow.

**Python**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or list of dictionaries for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).
* Optional configuration like [input preprocessing](#format-dataset-rows-before-evaluating).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against a [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) object or any custom function containing LLM application logic. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

**TypeScript**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or array of objects for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against any function wrapped with `weave.op`. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The TypeScript SDK uses function-based models and scorers. Class-based `Model` and `Scorer` types are not yet available in TypeScript.

To get started with evaluations, complete the following steps:

1. [Create an `Evaluation` object](#create-an-evaluation-object)
2. [Define a dataset of examples](#define-a-dataset-of-test-examples)
3. [Define scoring functions](#define-scoring-functions)
4. [Define a model or function to evaluate](#define-a-model-or-function-to-evaluate)
5. [Run the evaluation](#run-the-evaluation)

After completing these steps, you'll have a reusable evaluation configuration and an evaluation run whose results you can inspect in the Weights & Biases UI. For a complete evaluation code sample, see the [full evaluation code example](#full-evaluation-code-example). You can also learn more about [advanced evaluation features](#advanced-evaluation-usage) like [Saved views](#saved-views) and [Imperative evaluations](#imperative-evaluations-evaluationlogger).

# Integrations overview

> Trace agents and LLM applications with Weave's integrations for agent SDKs, harnesses, LLM providers, and orchestration frameworks.

Weave provides two ways to integrate with your AI stack:

* **Trace agents**: for multi-turn agentic applications built with agent SDKs (such as the OpenAI Agents SDK or Google ADK) or run inside agent harnesses (such as Claude Code, Codex, or Pi.dev). These integrations capture sessions, turns, LLM calls, and tool calls, and render them in the Weave **Agents** view.
* **Trace LLM applications**: for code that calls LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, and others) or uses orchestration frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, DSPy, and others). These integrations capture individual LLM calls and pipeline steps as Weave **Calls** in the **Traces** view.

If you're not sure which path to take, start with [Trace your agents](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/trace-agents.md) for new multi-turn agent work, or [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) for existing LLM-call workflows.

In short: tracing records what your application or agent does. Evaluations test it before release against a fixed set of examples. Signals score real conversations in production. All three work from what Weave records, but each answers a different question.

**1. Tracing: what happened**
- Weave's tracing is built on Ops, Calls, Traces and Threads. A **Trace** is the full tree of Calls (individual function or model calls) that share one execution context [S3, S5].
- Agent integrations, such as the OpenAI Agents SDK, Google ADK or Claude Code, record sessions, turns, LLM calls and tool calls, and show them in the **Agents** view. LLM-app integrations record Calls in the **Traces** view instead [S7].

**2. Evaluations: how well it works on known test cases**
- An `Evaluation` object combines a dataset of test examples with one or more scoring functions. You run it against a model or function, and each `.evaluate()` call is one evaluation run [S2].
- Use evaluations to measure performance on repeatable test cases, compare changes over time and catch regressions (drops in quality after a change) [S2].

**3. Signals: how it behaves in production**
- In the Agents view, the **Signals** tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations [S1]. To open it, select your project, choose **Agents** in the sidebar, then choose **Signals** [S6].
- A **rating** is a score from 0.0 to 1.0. **Tags** are labels such as "user-frustration" or "nsfw". Both are applied per **turn** (one user–agent exchange) [S4].
- Signals point out quality and safety problems and the traces that need attention [S1].

**How they connect (my inference):** tracing gives you the recorded data. Evaluations check changes against curated examples before release. Signals keep scoring live agent traffic and lead you to the specific problem traces. Those findings can then guide what you test in your next evaluation.

# Monitor using built-in signals

> Weights & Biases provides built-in scoring solutions for agents in production

> [!NOTE]
>
> This page covers a previous approach to monitoring production traffic. For new implementations, use **Signals** under Weave for Agents. See [View agent signals](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-signals.md).

Standard system metrics like latency, token count, and cost don't fully capture agent behavior. Inspecting individual traces provides deep insight but doesn't scale to the millions of traces generated in a live environment.

Signals provide a high-level monitoring solution to this problem by offering automated, behavioral scoring for agents in production:

* Automated scoring: Every incoming production trace is automatically processed and scored on common quality issues and errors.
* Infrastructure: Processing is powered by CoreWeave compute and CoreWeave GPUs for scalability across millions of traces.

By using signals within production, you can:

* Gain behavioral insight. Move beyond system metrics to understand if your agent is hallucinating, failing to follow conversation patterns, or losing grounding in its evidence.
* Accelerate the research loop. Use the scores and failure analyses generated by signals to identify weaknesses, which you can use to research model improvement, data annotation, or reinforcement learning.

## Available signals

Weave offers monitors with built-in signals: preset scorers that evaluate production traces for common quality issues and errors by default, with no custom setup. Each built-in signal uses a benchmarked LLM prompt to classify traces and saves the results as comma-delimited tags representing the detected issues.

Signals use a [Serverless Inference](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/inference/serverless.md) model to score traces, so you don't need external API keys.

Weave provides 13 preset signals organized into two groups.

## Signals and custom monitors

Use [signals](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/monitors.md), preset automated scorers for production traces, to get started with production monitoring quickly, then add custom monitors for evaluation criteria specific to your application.

| - | - | - |
| **Configuration** | One-click enable, no prompt writing | Full control over scoring prompt, model, and parameters |
| **Scope** | Preset quality and error classifiers | Any evaluation criteria you define |
| **Trace selection** | Automatic (successful root traces for quality, failed traces for errors) | Configurable operations, filters, and sampling rate |
| **Model** | Serverless Inference (preset) | Any commercial or Serverless Inference model |
| **Use case** | Quick production monitoring with proven classifiers | Custom evaluation criteria specific to your application |

# Set up custom monitors

> Passively score production traffic to surface trends and issues

> [!NOTE]
>
> Custom monitors are the previous approach to monitoring production traffic. For new implementations, use **Signals** under Weave for Agents. See [View agent signals](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-signals.md).

This page shows you how to set up custom monitors in Weave so you can passively score production traffic and surface trends and issues in your LLM applications. Use this guide when you want to define your own evaluation criteria, beyond Weave's preset signals, for production traces.

Monitors use LLM judges to passively score production traffic to surface trends and issues in your LLM applications. For example, you can monitor your application's responses for correctness or helpfulness, or you can monitor user input to identify trends in what users ask your agents about. Monitors automatically store all scoring results in Weave's database, so you can analyze historical trends and patterns.

You can monitor text, images, and audio in your application's input and output.

Monitors require no code changes to your application. Set them up using the Weights & Biases UI.

If you need to actively intervene in your application's behavior based on scores, use [guardrails](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/guardrails.md) instead.

To score calls with an HTTP endpoint that you host instead of an LLM judge, see [Score Calls with remote scorers](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/remote-scorers.md).

result.heading: Calls
result.text:
## Calls

A **Call** is a logged execution of an Op. Every time an Op runs, Weave creates a Call that captures:

* Input arguments
* Output value
* Timing and latency
* Parent-child relationships (for nested calls)
* Any errors that occur

Calls show up as **Traces** in the Weights & Biases UI and provide the data for debugging, analysis, and evaluation. For the full Call object structure and properties, see the [Call schema reference](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/call-schema-reference.md).

Calls are similar to spans in the [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io) data model. A Call can:

* Belong to a Trace, a collection of Calls in the same execution context.
* Have parent and child Calls, forming a tree structure.
